H2.1: The roll rate peaks early and sags while the stick is still held because the aircraft starts to slide right and the dihedral effect rolls it back (L_v about −0.2 rad/s² per m/s in the hover, of the size DLR identified for the type). Same data and verdict as in the second flight.
H2.2: Same mechanism as H2.1: the sideways drift the pulse starts rolls the aircraft back through the dihedral effect, so the bank is not held. A hingeless rotor with no stability augmentation does this; the card's rate-response picture fits an aircraft with the drift held.
H2.5: No pedal input; the yaw is the drift. The yaw moment budget of the recording: as the aircraft slides right at up to 2.4 m/s, the air coming sideways into the Fenestron lowers its thrust by 4 % (1.52 to 1.46 kN), the rotor's torque wins by 0.25 kNm and the nose follows the drift. With the drift held at zero the same pulse yaws the aircraft not at all. The model's N_v in the hover (0.016 1/(m·s) linearised, ~0.023 at 2 m/s) is a third to a half of the BO 105's near the hover (Heffley 1979, 10 kt: 0.047), so the effect is not overstated; the card's |r| < 5 °/s would need the drift below about 1.3 m/s.
H3.1: Same recording as in the second flight, which was rated PASS: the fitted pitch time constant is 0.415 s against 0.45–0.85 s. The model is quicker in pitch than the published bandwidth (KNOWN in the test suite). 2.3 traced it to a short-period mode that is quicker and has less delay than the aircraft's; the stabiliser, which the type's designers sized for good angle-of-attack stability and pitch damping, is not the cause (docs/TECHNICAL.md).
H4.2: The decay is not first order, and the yaw moment budget of the recording shows why. When the pedal returns at 4 s the Fenestron goes back to its trim thrust plus its damping, but the rotor speed dips (99.4 %) as the cabin's yaw slows, and the governor's extra torque (+0.7 kNm at the mast) reacts on the cabin in the sense it was turning: with the rotor speed governed, the rotor's polar inertia (2000 kg m²) joins the yaw axis. The model's aerodynamic yaw damping is −0.56 1/s against about −0.5 identified for the EC135 by DLR, whose model carries the rotor speed as a state of its own. A fifth of the rate left at 6 s comes from the sideways drift the step leaves (with the drift held at zero: 19.6 instead of 25.1 °/s). No EC135 hover yaw time history was found to settle it.
H6.4: The first nose-up peak is 0.785° against 0.8–2°; the rest of the sequence matches. Same recording as in the second and third flight.
H7.3: From a hover with the lever down, the flat-pitch rotor still needs 20–28 kW until about 3.5 s, and the Fenestron, with the pedals fixed, keeps taking 16 kW: together they bring the rotor speed down by about 2 %/s. The rotor only starts to drive itself at about 3.8 s and 3,300 fpm, as the empirical curve of induced velocity in descent (Leishman) has it: a rotor windmills only beyond about 1.8–1.9 times the hover induced velocity for the thrust it carries. In addition the cabin spins left at about 150 °/s, which lowers the rotor speed relative to the cabin, what the gauge shows, by about 6 % of NR. A pilot's right pedal would take most of the fan's share away; the card holds the pedals.
F1.3: The ratio is high because the hover power is low (442 kW, the bottom of the author's 440–570 kW band), not because the cruise power is high: 584 kW at 135 kt is inside its band, and the drag that sets it is calibrated to the published 137 kt at maximum continuous power.
F1.5: The collective follows the power (F1.3). For the BO 105, the EC135's predecessor with a similar hingeless rotor, the trim collective at 135 kt is about 3.4° above the hover value (Heffley 1979); the card's band is the author's estimate. The second flight had +3.8° and was rated NEAR.
F3.3: The first yaw comes from the product of inertia (I_xz, 650 kg m² in the model, an estimate): it turns a right roll acceleration into a nose-right yaw acceleration. The aerodynamic yaw due to roll rate at 100 kt is adverse (N_p −0.79 1/s in the model) and shows as the −1.2 °/s once the roll rate steadies and the stick returns. Neither I_xz nor N_p is published for the type; the second flight had the same shape and was rated NEAR.
F6.2: The minimum, 83.7 %, comes at 2.85 s, a few tenths of a second after the expected 1.2–2.5 s, during the −0.23 g push the fixed cyclic gives at the failure. With the collective full down (as the plan says, since 2.2) the steady autorotation turns at 110.8 %, inside the card's 95–112 % but above the 106 % power-off limit a pilot would hold with the collective.
F7.3: Blade torsion (2.1) now limits the stall: the bank change at 3 s fell from −112° to −56°, and the aircraft rolls back by 5 s. In an abrupt pull-up from 140 kt the peak blade loading matches Kampa's limit at the same advance ratio within 1 % (VAL in the test suite since 2.3); local stall begins at about 1.2 g, well below that limit, which leaves time for the roll to build. Until 2.2 that onset was compared with the 1.7 g of the limit as a KNOWN deviation: two different things.
F9.4: In ball-centred flight the tail's anti-torque side force has to be taken by the fuselage (sideslip) or by a lateral tilt of the rotor thrust, and the hingeless rotor's hub moment keeps that tilt small. With the fuselage side force set to the derivative breakdown of Kampa et al. 1997 (Fig. 18), level flight at 100 kt needs 3.4°; the turn adds little (the second flight: 5.9°).
